opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. The way we think about it, the robot itself isn't really the product; the outcome is. Most of the customers we talk to, whether in manufacturing, logistics, or other industrial settings, don't want to make a big capital bet on a technology they haven't seen work on their own floor. So for the initial deployments we lean toward a service-style model, essentially robots-as-a-service. The customer pays for the labor the robot provides, on a recurring basis, rather than buying a machine outright.

That does a few things for us. First, it lowers the barrier to entry. A plant manager can say yes to a pilot without going through a long capex approval cycle. Second, it keeps us accountable. If we're getting paid for performance and uptime, we have every incentive to make sure the robot keeps working, keeps improving, and actually delivers value. Third, it gives us a tight feedback loop. We're on site, we're seeing where the robot struggles, and that data goes straight back into improving the hardware and the software.

We're also deliberate about which jobs we go after first. We look for tasks that are dull, dirty, or dangerous, where companies have trouble hiring and retaining people, and where the work is structured enough that we can be reliable early. Labor shortages are real in a lot of these industries, so when we price, we benchmark against the fully loaded cost of a worker in that role, and we aim to come in at or below it while offering more hours of availability.

Over time, as volumes go up and unit costs come down, the economics only get better, and we'll likely offer more flexibility, including outright purchase for customers who want it. But early on, aligning our revenue with the customer's results is the best way to build trust and prove that humanoid robots can do real, productive work.

r001.rationale: The response does not mention a small customer roster or a 100-robot minimum deployment per customer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses pricing relative to worker costs and future flexibility, but does not say per-robot prices will rise as robots take on harder jobs.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest answer is that we started from the customer's accounting department, not from the robot. If you walk into a manufacturing plant or a logistics operation and say, "Here's a humanoid, write me a check for a few hundred thousand dollars," you've already lost. The capital expense committee doesn't know how to underwrite a robot. They don't know the useful life, they don't know the maintenance curve, and frankly neither do we yet with full certainty. So asking them to take that risk on a first-generation product is a non-starter.

What they do know how to underwrite is labor. Every one of these facilities has a line item for the roles they can't fill, the overtime they're paying, the turnover costs, the workers' comp exposure on the dangerous or repetitive jobs. So we structure the early deployments as robots-as-a-service. You pay a monthly rate that maps to the task the robot is doing, we retain ownership of the hardware, we handle maintenance, software updates, and swaps if a unit goes down. The customer's decision becomes a simple comparison: what does this cost me per hour against what I'm paying today, including all the hidden costs of not being able to staff the shift.

There are a few reasons that works for us too, not just for them. One, it keeps the fleet in our hands, which means we're constantly getting data back and iterating. A robot you've sold outright and lost visibility into is a robot you can't learn from. Two, it aligns incentives. If the robot sits idle, we don't get paid for that time, so we're motivated to make sure it's actually productive, not just impressive in a demo. And three, it lets us be very deliberate about which deployments we take. We're not trying to be everywhere in year one. We're picking a small number of partners where the task is well-scoped, the environment is somewhat structured, and the customer is willing to be a real collaborator, because the first deployments are as much about us learning as about them saving money.

The longer-term vision is that as reliability data accumulates and the cost curve comes down with volume, you start to see more flexibility, maybe outright purchase for some customers, maybe hybrid models. But I think the mistake a lot of people in this space make is leading with the technology story and hoping the business model sorts itself out. We tried to do it the other way around. Figure out how the customer actually buys, then build the offering to fit that, and let the robot be the thing that makes the economics work rather than the thing we're asking them to believe in.

r001.rationale: The response says it is selecting a small number of partners, but does not attribute that roster to a minimum deployment of 100 robots per customer.

r002.rationale: It discusses monthly task-based pricing and possible future sales models, but does not say per-robot prices will rise as robots take on harder jobs.

astra-6.text:
The way I’d approach it is to start with a very specific job and a clear return for the customer. What does that job cost today, and can the robot do it reliably enough to deliver real savings once you include deployment, maintenance, and support?

For those initial deployments, I’d favor a service model that lowers the customer’s upfront commitment and keeps us accountable for performance. Start small, prove the economics in the customer’s actual environment, and expand from there. The commercial proposition has to be about useful work delivered.

r001.rationale: The response recommends starting small but does not attribute a small customer roster to a 100-robot minimum deployment.

r002.rationale: It discusses customer savings and a service model, but does not say per-robot prices will rise as the robots take on harder jobs.

sol-6.1.text: We approach it around the value the robot can deliver in a specific job. What is the customer paying to get that work done today, and can we do it reliably at a price that makes sense for them? For those initial deployments, the priority is proving that economics in a real operating environment. Then you have a foundation for a commercial model that can scale.

r001.rationale: The response discusses proving the economics of initial deployments but does not attribute a small customer roster to a 100-robot minimum per customer.

r002.rationale: The response discusses pricing that makes sense for customers but does not say per-robot prices will rise as robots take on harder jobs.
